De passage au Québec, l’ingénieure aéros: During a visit to Quebec, aerospace engineer Farah Alibay is on every platform. Now celebrated across the province as the Quebecer at NASA who steers a robot on Mars, she is inspiring young racialized women to follow in her footsteps. We spoke with her, then went to meet Quebec’s future Farahs.
<strong>‍</strong>Le parcours de Farah,: ‍Farah, who is of Malagasy origin, has not always had an easy path. “There were really times, growing up, when I wasn’t sure I would be accepted in society,” she tells us at the C2 Montréal conference. Already, I work in a field that’s dominated by men… and on top of that there’s the culture and the skin colour – it can be exhausting.”
Les doutes, les remises en question, le: Doubt, self-questioning, impostor syndrome and failure all came up along the way. As a teenager, a guidance counsellor tried to discourage her from going into engineering. As a young adult, she failed every course in her first university semester. During her studies, she sent out more than twenty applications to NASA before receiving an internship offer. At work, she endured a manager’s sexism. Like “little cuts,” sexism and racism marked her academic and professional path. “There were times when I asked myself: ‘Why am I pursuing this dream?’” Farah Alibay tells us. But her desire to explore space pushed her to persevere.
« Chaque fois qu’on me disait quelque ch: “Every time someone told me something I didn’t feel like hearing, what helped me was finding that passion within myself again.” Today, she considers herself lucky to have moved past her doubts. “I was lucky to get past that, and I know we lose an enormous number of women, an enormous number of people of colour because of it – because we aren’t encouraged, because we can’t find our place in our field.” Farah says that when she lived in Quebec, she lacked mentors and role models she could see herself in. “I watched Apollo 13, and I noticed that everyone looked the same. I didn’t even allow myself to dream of one day working at NASA,” she says. Today, she wants to use the platforms she’s being offered to give young women the role model she never had.
« Je veux montrer aux gens que tu ne doi: “I want to show people that you don’t have to look a certain way to follow your dreams and get to a certain place. I want to show them what it takes so they can follow their dreams. And yes, it forced me to leave Quebec and do something big. But my example shows that there are women like me in these positions and that it generates interest from the public and the media. And what’s more, you don’t only find them in such roles in the United States and elsewhere in the world, but also here in Quebec. I’m happy to be able to offer something different to young people today.”
En février dernier, lorsque le robot Per: Last February, when the Perseverance rover landed on Mars, the whole world discovered an aerospace engineer from Joliette. Many racialized women in Quebec saw themselves in her.
Jenin Islam, étudiante à l'École seconda: Jenin Islam, student at École secondaire Cavelier-de-Lasalle
Étudiante en 5e secondaire, Jenin Islam: A Secondary 5 student, Jenin Islam wants to study science, but she doesn’t yet know in which field. Like many women who hope to go into science, the teenager went to meet Farah Alibay at the École de technologie supérieure last Thursday evening.
Son professeur de robotique lui a consei: Her robotics teacher advised her to attend a science communication workshop at the conference for girls in STEM. “My teachers and my family encourage me to go into this field; what scares me is the pressure. I’m not good at math, but biology and programming interest me,” she says after leaving the workshop. When she sees Farah Alibay’s path, the 16-year-old student manages to picture her future in STEM with a little more confidence. “I tell myself that if she can do it, I’ll definitely try too, and maybe I’ll make it too.”
Jade Tremblay Mainville, étudiante en sc: Jade Tremblay Mainville, natural science student at Collège de l'Assomption.‍Photo: Lela Savic
Jade Tremblay Mainville est étudiante au: Jade Tremblay Mainville is a natural science student at Collège de l’Assomption. “Farah’s whole story really influenced me to persevere in the world of science,” she confides. “I’d like to take people somewhere else. Unlike a lot of people around me, I’m not necessarily the best at physics and chemistry, but I’m so passionate!” she says enthusiastically. Like Farah, Jade grew up in Joliette. Adopted at a year and a half old, the young woman of Asian origin feels drawn to the aerospace engineer’s path.
«Mais je ne me vois pas aller aussi loin: “But I can’t see myself going as far as she did. Sometimes, when I go to the store, people look at me sideways because I’m of Asian origin. But knowing that Farah comes from Joliette like me makes things feel more accessible,” explains the 17-year-old student.

Sadia Hussein, étudiante en génie logici: Sadia Hussein, software engineering student at ÉTS Photo: Lela Savic
« C’est un symbole qu’on a tous une Fara: “It’s a symbol that we all have a Farah in us,” says engineering student Sadia Hussein passionately after hearing the doctoral student talk about her journey. “We didn’t all grow up in Joliette, but we just need to persevere and it’s not too late. Because of course we can tell ourselves: ‘I didn’t go study in England or at MIT, but that’s okay. We all have a Farah in us, we just need to want to do it,” she exclaims. Hearing the aerospace engineer’s message motivates her. “As Farah said, the worst that can happen is that in the end, I don’t succeed, but the best that can happen is that I achieve my dream.”
Sadia Hussein est étudiante en génie log: Sadia Hussein is a software engineering student at ÉTS. Since she was 10, she has dreamed of being a software engineer.
Aujourd’hui, elle fait partie des Ingéni: Today, she is part of Les Ingénieuses, a group of women in engineering. During her high school and CEGEP years, she was often told she “didn’t have the profile of an engineer” because she is very sociable. Even now, she feels that her colleagues and professors doubt her abilities because she is a woman. “We always need to prove we’re capable, whereas for guys, it’s as if it’s innate,” she says.
Aujourd’hui en troisième année de bac, e: Now in the third year of her bachelor’s degree, she wonders whether she belongs in this environment, whether she’s on the right path. Moreover, the few women who are with her in STEM don’t look like her, she tells us. “A lot of them are privileged white women,” she says, before adding that her background is not the same. “Some of them come from private schools, and I come from public school.
Est-ce que je suis au même niveau qu’ell: Am I at the same level as them? I feel so much like I’m lacking resources. Sometimes I tell myself I’ll never make it. I don’t see women like me,” says the 23-year-old student. After hearing Farah talk about her failures, her doubts and her journey, she burst into tears. “Me, who’s not an aerospace engineer, who’s nothing right now, I’m able to understand what Farah went through; it really touched me. It touched me to see that I’m not alone in this.
She went through the same problems as me. She also felt alone, she was also a member of a minority in her neighbourhood, in her school, she also had problems, difficulties, but she persevered. It really struck me and I told myself: ‘Me too, I can do it.’ It’s normal to doubt yourself,” she says with emotion.
<strong>« Farah, pour moi, c’est quelqu’: “To me, Farah is someone who looks like me”
Farah Alibay et Zeina Marhan,étudiante e: Farah Alibay and Zeina Marhan, natural science student at Dawson College. Photo: Lela Savic
Zeina Mahran est étudiante au Collège Da: Zeina Mahran is a natural science student at Dawson College. It has only been a year since she discovered a passion for engineering. When she shares her ambition with those around her, they ask if she’s sure of her choice. “Often, people don’t believe me. They ask me if it’s not my parents forcing me to go into this field,” she reports.
Elle ajoute qu’au cours de son parcours: She adds that over the course of her schooling, she was not encouraged to go into scientific fields. “It just wasn’t a possibility; nobody destroyed my dream, but they didn’t give me that option, which existed,” the student says. She believes girls are generally encouraged to go into other fields, notably health, on the pretext that they like taking care of others. The 19-year-old questions those ideas.
« On dit souvent aux petits garçons qu’i: “Little boys are often told they’re going to become engineers, little girls are never told that, and that has to change,” says Zeina Mahran indignantly. But without female role models, it’s hard for her to picture herself as an engineer. “So when I see women in those positions, it plants a little seed in my head, it tells me it’s a possibility. It gives me hope and lets me believe I have a place in engineering.” Farah Alibay gave her even more hope of achieving her dream. “To me, Farah is someone who looks like me. Even though we don’t have the same origins, she’s a racialized woman, she inspires me. When I see her, it gives me hope of one day finding myself in a position like hers,” she tells us after hearing the aerospace engineer’s talk at G-Change at the École de technologie supérieure.
Dans la province, à peine 15 % des 65 00: In the province, barely 15% of the 65,000 members of the Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec (OIQ) are women, explains the order’s president, Kathy Baig. The rate of newly registered women engineers is 20%. The OIQ would like to raise the rate of new women engineers to 30% by 2030. What does Farah Alibay advise those who want to study science, technology, engineering and mathematics? “You have to know what your passion is, focus on that and forget the other voices.
J’en ai plein, des gens qui m’ont dit :: I’ve had plenty of people tell me: ‘No, you won’t succeed in that field where there’s no place for you.’ You have to understand that for every yes, there are going to be dozens of nos – you have to prepare for that. But above all, you have to find your curiosity and go for it, dive right in. You’ll see, it’s so worth it to live your dream!” Dreams that, we hope, will not be shattered by adversity.
